g.text: Everything in JavaScript happens inside an Execution Context.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Execution Context is the foundational concept of JavaScript. Before a single line of your code runs, the JS engine creates an environment — the Execution Context — that manages all variable storage and code execution.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Think of it as a big container (box) with two compartments inside it. Every time JavaScript runs code, it does so within one of these containers.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Understanding Execution Context is the key to understanding hoisting, closures, scope, and the call stack — almost every advanced JS concept builds on this foundation.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is an Execution Context?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: An Execution Context is an environment where JavaScript code is evaluated and executed. It has two components: Memory (Variable Environment) and Code (Thread of Execution).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What are the two phases of an Execution Context?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Phase 1 is the Memory Creation Phase where variables get undefined and functions get stored fully. Phase 2 is the Code Execution Phase where code runs line by line.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is the Global Execution Context?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The GEC is the default context created when a JS program starts. All top-level code runs in the GEC. There is only one GEC per program.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Why is JS called single-threaded?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Because it has only one Call Stack — it can do only one thing at a time.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Call Stack is JavaScript's mechanism for managing multiple Execution Contexts.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a JS program runs, a Global Execution Context (GEC) is created. But what happens when a function is called inside that program? A new Execution Context is created for it. And if that function calls another function? Yet another one.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript needs a way to keep track of all these contexts — to know which one is currently running, and which ones are waiting. That mechanism is the Call Stack.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Call Stack is a stack data structure that tracks Execution Contexts. It follows LIFO — Last In, First Out. The most recently created context is at the top, and it must finish before the one below it resumes.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Other names you may hear for the Call Stack:

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When the program starts → GEC is created and pushed onto the Call Stack

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a function is called → a new Execution Context is created and pushed on top

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a function returns → its Execution Context is popped off the stack

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When the program finishes → GEC is popped off and the stack is empty

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Each Execution Context goes through two phases:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Memory Creation Phase: JS scans the code, allocates memory for variables (undefined) and stores full function bodies

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Code Execution Phase: Code runs line by line; variable values are assigned; function calls push new contexts

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: If functions call each other infinitely (e.g. unbounded recursion), the Call Stack fills up completely. This results in a Stack Overflow error — the engine throws a Maximum call stack size exceeded error.

g.text: Q: What is the Call Stack?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The Call Stack is a stack data structure used by the JS engine to manage Execution Contexts. It follows LIFO — the last context pushed is the first to be popped.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What happens to the Call Stack when a function is called?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: A new Execution Context is created for that function and pushed onto the top of the Call Stack. When the function returns, its context is popped off.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is a Stack Overflow?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: When recursion (or repeated function calls) fills the Call Stack beyond its limit, the engine throws a RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. This is called a Stack Overflow.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What other names does the Call Stack go by?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Execution Context Stack, Program Stack, Control Stack, Runtime Stack, Machine Stack.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Call Stack manages all Execution Contexts using LIFO order

g.text: Every function call pushes a new EC; every return pops it

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Call Stack is always visible in browser DevTools — use it for debugging

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Unbounded recursion causes Stack Overflow (Maximum call stack size exceeded)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JS has only ONE call stack — it can only do one thing at a time

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Hoisting lets you access variables and call functions before they appear in the source code — because of how the Memory Creation Phase works.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Hoisting is one of JavaScript's most misunderstood behaviors. Newcomers expect code to run strictly top-to-bottom, so accessing a variable before its declaration looks like it should throw an error. Instead, JS often returns undefined or even the full function — which seems like magic.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The explanation is the Execution Context's two-phase model: memory is allocated before any code runs. By the time line 1 executes, all variables and functions are already in memory. That's hoisting.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When the JS engine encounters var x = 5;, during Phase 1 (memory allocation) it stores x → undefined. The actual assignment (x = 5) only happens in Phase 2 when that line is reached.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This means accessing x before the assignment gives undefined, not an error.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Function declarations are stored completely in memory during Phase 1 — the entire function body is available. This means you can call a function before its definition in the code.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a function is assigned to a variable (var fn = function() {}), it follows variable hoisting rules — the variable gets undefined in Phase 1, not the function body.

g.text: let and const — Temporal Dead Zone

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: let and const are also hoisted, but they are placed in a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) — a special state where the variable exists in memory but cannot be accessed until its declaration line is reached. Accessing them before their declaration throws a ReferenceError.

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Hoisting is a behavior where variable declarations and function declarations are conceptually "moved" to the top of their scope before code executes. In reality, memory is allocated for them in Phase 1 of Execution Context creation.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is the value of a var variable before its assignment line?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: undefined. The variable exists in memory (from Phase 1) but its assigned value hasn't been set yet.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Can you call a function before its declaration?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Yes — for function declarations. Their entire body is stored in Phase 1. But function expressions assigned to var variables cannot be called before the assignment line.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What happens if you access a let or const variable before its declaration?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: A ReferenceError is thrown because let/const are in the Temporal Dead Zone until their declaration line is reached.

g.text: Hoisting is a result of the Memory Creation Phase (Phase 1) of Execution Context

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: var variables are hoisted with value undefined

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Function declarations are hoisted with their full body — callable anywhere in scope

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Function expressions (var fn = function() {}) follow var hoisting — the variable is undefined until assigned

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: let and const are hoisted but sit in the Temporal Dead Zone — accessing them early throws ReferenceError

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Always declare variables at the top of their scope to avoid hoisting surprises

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Each function call creates its own Execution Context with its own Variable Environment — variables don't leak between calls.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This episode connects the dots between what we know about Execution Contexts and how functions actually behave at runtime. When a function is invoked, a fresh Execution Context is created for it — complete with its own memory space. Multiple calls to the same function each get their own isolated Variable Environment.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This is what makes local variables truly local, and it's the foundation of closures, scope chains, and the call stack behavior we've seen.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Each Function Call Gets Its Own Execution Context

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When JavaScript invokes a function, the engine:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Creates a new Execution Context (EC) for that function

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Pushes it onto the Call Stack

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Runs Phase 1 (memory allocation) for that EC — local variables start as undefined

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Runs Phase 2 (code execution) — assignment and logic runs

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Returns the result; the EC is popped from the Call Stack and destroyed

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Each EC has its own Variable Environment. A variable named x in one function call has no connection to a variable named x in another call — even if they're calls to the same function. They live in separate memory spaces.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The GEC is always the bottommost context on the Call Stack. Code at the top level of a file executes inside the GEC. Function calls create ECs on top of the GEC — those ECs can reference the GEC's variables (via scope chain), but the GEC cannot reach into a function's local EC.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a function executes return ans, the value is passed back to the calling context (the EC below on the stack). The function's EC is then immediately deleted. The variable in the calling context receives the returned value.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What happens inside the JS engine when a function is called?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: A new Execution Context is created for that function call. It goes through Phase 1 (memory allocation for local variables) and Phase 2 (code execution). The EC is pushed onto the Call Stack when the function starts, and popped when it returns.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Does a function's local variable affect variables outside it?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: No. Each function has its own Variable Environment (memory space). A var x inside a function is completely separate from a var x outside it.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What happens to a function's EC after it returns?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The EC is popped off the Call Stack and destroyed. All local variables in it are gone (unless captured in a closure).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Can GEC variables be accessed inside a function?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Yes — functions can access variables from outer scopes via the scope chain. But the GEC cannot access variables that are local to a function.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Every function call creates a fresh, independent Execution Context

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Local variables live in the function's Variable Environment and are isolated from other ECs

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The same function called twice creates two separate ECs — they don't share memory

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a function returns, its EC is destroyed — local variables are cleaned up

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Call Stack manages the order of ECs: GEC at the bottom, active function EC at the top

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This isolation is fundamental to how scope and closures work in JavaScript

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Episode 5: Shortest JS Program, Window & this Keyword

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: An empty JavaScript file is still a valid program — the engine creates a Global Execution Context, a window object, and a this binding before running a single line of your code.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: What does JavaScript do when given a completely empty file? More than you'd expect. The JS engine automatically sets up the Global Execution Context, creates the window global object, and establishes the this keyword — all before any user code runs.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This episode unpacks what those things are and why they exist.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: An empty .js file is the shortest valid JavaScript program. Even with zero lines of user code, the JS engine:

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Creates the window object (in browser environments)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Sets up the this keyword at the global level

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: window is a global object created by the JavaScript engine (specifically, by the browser's JS runtime). It represents the browser window and serves as the global scope container.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: All global variables and functions you declare become properties of window

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Built-in browser APIs (setTimeout, console, fetch, localStorage) are all properties of window

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: You can access window properties with or without the window. prefix

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: console.log(window.name); // "Namaste" — var globals attach to window

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: console.log(name); // "Namaste" — same thing, window. is implicit

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Note: In Node.js the global object is called global, not window. In modern environments, globalThis works universally.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The this Keyword at the Global Level

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: At the global level (outside any function), this refers to the global object:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: console.log(this === window); // true (in browsers, at global scope)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This is important to understand because this changes value depending on where and how it's used — but at the top level, it always points to the global object.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When you declare a variable with var at the top level (not inside any function), it becomes a property of the window object:

g.text: Q: What is the shortest JavaScript program?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: An empty file. Even with no user code, the engine creates the GEC, window object, and this binding.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is the window object?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The window object is the global object in browser environments. It contains all global variables (declared with var), built-in browser APIs, and is the value of this at the global scope.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What does this equal at the global scope in a browser?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: this equals the window object. this === window is true at the global level.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Do let and const variables attach to the window object?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: No. Only var variables declared at the global level become properties of window. let and const create global variables but don't attach to the global object.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: globalThis is a standardized way (ES2020) to access the global object across all environments — whether browser (window), Node.js (global), or web workers (self).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JS engine creates GEC, window, and this even for an empty file

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The global object differs per environment: window (browser), global (Node.js), globalThis (universal)

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: undefined is a value JavaScript assigns to variables that exist but haven't been given a value yet. "Not defined" means the variable doesn't exist at all.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript has a special value called undefined that is distinct from an error. Beginners often confuse undefined with "not defined" — but they are fundamentally different things. One is a valid value; the other is a runtime error.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Understanding this distinction also deepens your understanding of the Memory Creation Phase and how JavaScript reserves space for variables before executing code.

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: During Phase 1 (Memory Creation) of the Execution Context, JavaScript allocates memory for every variable it finds in the code and assigns each one the special value undefined as a placeholder.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This means undefined is an actual value — it is the "not yet assigned" state of a variable.

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: If you try to access a variable that was never declared anywhere in the code, JavaScript cannot find it in any scope. The engine throws a ReferenceError: x is not defined.

g.text: Using undefined as a Value — Avoid This

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This is considered bad practice because it defeats the purpose of undefined as a signal that no value has been assigned. Use null when you want to explicitly represent "no value".

g.text: Q: What is undefined in JavaScript?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: undefined is a primitive value that JavaScript automatically assigns to variables during the Memory Creation Phase (Phase 1). It means the variable exists in memory but hasn't been given a value yet.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: "Not defined" is a ReferenceError thrown when you try to access a variable that was never declared. The engine cannot find it in any scope.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is the difference between undefined and null?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: undefined is set by the JS engine automatically as a placeholder. null is explicitly set by the programmer to represent an intentional absence of value.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Yes. undefined is one of JavaScript's falsy values, along with null, 0, '', false, and NaN.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: undefined is a real value that JS assigns during the Memory Creation Phase

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: "Not defined" is a ReferenceError — the variable was never declared

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: undefined !== null — both represent "empty" but mean different things

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Never deliberately assign undefined to a variable — use null instead

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: undefined is falsy — it evaluates to false in boolean contexts

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Use typeof x === 'undefined' for the safest undefined-check (works even on undeclared variables)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Scope determines where a variable can be accessed. Lexical Environment is the mechanism that makes scope work — each Execution Context carries a reference to its parent's memory.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Scope is directly related to the Lexical Environment. Every time an Execution Context is created, a Lexical Environment is also created alongside it. This Lexical Environment consists of the local memory of the current EC plus a reference to the Lexical Environment of its parent.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This chaining of environments — from child to parent to grandparent, all the way up to the GEC — is called the Scope Chain. It is how JavaScript resolves variable names.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A Lexical Environment is composed of:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Local memory — all variables/functions declared in the current scope

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: "Lexical" means "in order of the source code" — where something is written determines its parent's environment.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Lexical Environment = Local Memory + Ref to Parent's Lexical Env

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Every Execution Context has a Lexical Environment. The GEC's Lexical Environment has a parent reference of null (it has no parent).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When JavaScript encounters a variable name, it looks for it:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: First in the local memory of the current EC

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: If not found, follows the parent reference to the parent's Lexical Environment

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Keeps going up the chain until it finds the variable or reaches the GEC

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: If not found in GEC either → ReferenceError

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This traversal is the Scope Chain (also called the Lexical Environment Chain).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript uses lexical scope — a function's scope is determined by where it is written in the source code, not by where it is called from.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: inner can access x not because it was called from inside outer, but because it was written (defined) inside outer. The lexical nesting is what matters.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Variables declared at the top level (in the GEC) have global scope. They are accessible from anywhere in the program — from any function, any nested function, through the scope chain.

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is scope in JavaScript?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Scope defines the region of code where a variable is accessible. Variables declared in a function are scoped to that function; variables in the GEC are globally scoped.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is a Lexical Environment?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: A Lexical Environment is the combination of local memory (variables/functions in the current scope) plus a reference to the parent's Lexical Environment. It is created whenever an Execution Context is created.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is the Scope Chain?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The Scope Chain is the series of Lexical Environments linked together from child to parent. When a variable is not found locally, JS traverses the scope chain upward until it finds the variable or exhausts all environments.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What determines a function's scope in JavaScript?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Where the function is written (defined) in the source code — not where it is called from. This is called lexical scope (or static scope).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript uses lexical (static) scope — scope is determined at write-time, not call-time

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Variable lookup walks up the scope chain; failure to find results in ReferenceError

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: var is function-scoped; let/const are block-scoped

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Episode 8: let, const and the Temporal Dead Zone

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: let and const are hoisted differently from var — they live in a Temporal Dead Zone until their declaration line, making early access a ReferenceError.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: let and const were introduced in ES6 to fix several pain points with var. They bring stricter scoping rules (block scope instead of function scope) and stricter hoisting behavior (Temporal Dead Zone). Understanding when and why to use each — and what errors they produce — is essential for modern JavaScript.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: How let and const Are Hoisted

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: All three — var, let, and const — are hoisted. But they differ in where they are stored and whether they are accessible:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: var → stored in the global object (window) memory; initialized to undefined

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: let/const → stored in a separate memory space (not on window); placed in the Temporal Dead Zone

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: You can observe this in browser DevTools: before any code runs, var variables appear in the global scope, while let/const variables appear in a distinct "Script" scope — inaccessible until their declaration line is reached.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Temporal Dead Zone is the period from when a let/const variable is hoisted to when its declaration line is executed. During this time, the variable exists in memory but cannot be accessed.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: TDZ ends: (the let/const declaration line is reached)

g.text: Q: Are let and const hoisted?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Yes, they are hoisted — but they are placed in the Temporal Dead Zone rather than initialized to undefined. They cannot be accessed until their declaration line is reached.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is the Temporal Dead Zone?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The TDZ is the time between when a let/const variable is hoisted and when it is initialized. Accessing the variable during this period throws a ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization.

g.text: A: Both are block-scoped and have TDZ. The difference is that const cannot be reassigned after initialization and must be initialized when declared. let allows reassignment.

g.text: JavaScript's { } braces serve double duty: they group statements (forming a "compound statement") and they create a new block scope for let and const variables. Understanding how variables shadow each other across scopes — and where that shadowing becomes illegal — is crucial for writing predictable code.

g.text: A: A block is a pair of curly braces { } that groups multiple statements together. It is also called a compound statement. Blocks create a new scope for let and const variables.

g.text: A: Shadowing occurs when a variable in an inner scope has the same name as one in an outer scope. The inner variable "shadows" (hides) the outer one within its scope. The outer variable is not modified.

g.text: A: Illegal shadowing is when you try to shadow a let or const variable with a var in a nested block. It throws a SyntaxError because var would escape the block and conflict with the let/const in the outer scope.

g.text: A closure is a function bundled together with its lexical environment — it remembers the variables from its outer scope even after that outer function has returned.

g.text: Closures are one of the most powerful and most misunderstood features of JavaScript. They arise naturally from lexical scoping: when a function is defined inside another function, it carries a reference to the outer function's variables. Even after the outer function finishes executing, those variables remain alive in memory — kept there by the closure.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Closures enable powerful patterns: data encapsulation, factory functions, memoization, currying, and the module pattern. They also have costs: overuse can cause memory leaks.

g.text: More precisely: when a function is created, it captures a reference (not a copy) to its enclosing Lexical Environment. That environment persists as long as the function (closure) exists.

g.text: Over-consumption of memory: Closed-over variables cannot be garbage collected as long as the closure exists. Creating many closures around large objects can bloat memory.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Memory leaks: If a closure is accidentally kept alive (e.g., as an event listener that's never removed), the variables it closes over are never freed.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Can freeze the browser: Extreme cases of memory accumulation from closures can degrade browser performance.

g.text: Q: What is a closure in JavaScript?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: A closure is a function bundled together with a reference to its outer (lexical) environment. It allows the function to access variables from its enclosing scope even after that scope has returned.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What does a closure capture — a reference or a value?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: A reference. The closure points to the actual variable in the outer scope. If the variable changes, the closure sees the new value.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What are the advantages of closures?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Data hiding/encapsulation (module pattern), currying, memoization, maintaining state between function calls (counters), and working correctly with async operations like setTimeout.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What are the disadvantages of closures?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Overconsumption of memory (closed-over variables are not garbage collected while the closure lives), potential memory leaks if closures are not cleaned up, and potential performance issues in extreme cases.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A closure = function + its lexical environment (reference to outer scope's variables)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Closures allow a function to "remember" its outer variables even after the outer function returns

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Closures capture references, not snapshots — the values seen are live

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Key use cases: data privacy (module pattern), currying, memoization, counters, setTimeout

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Downside: closed-over variables persist in memory — can cause leaks if mismanaged

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Closures are not a special syntax — they arise naturally from lexical scoping

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Time, tide, and JavaScript wait for none — setTimeout does not pause execution, but closures can preserve the right values across asynchronous delays.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This episode is a classic interview question that catches many developers off guard. The combination of setTimeout and loops exposes a critical behavior: var in a loop shares a single binding across all iterations, while the setTimeout callbacks fire long after the loop is done. Closures with let — or an IIFE with var — are the solutions.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: setTimeout registers a callback to be called after a minimum delay. JavaScript does not wait for the timer — it continues executing the rest of the code immediately. The callback is placed in the Callback Queue and only runs when the Call Stack is empty.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Why? Because var i is function/globally scoped — all 5 setTimeout callbacks share the same i variable. By the time any callback fires (after 1s+), the loop has already finished and i is 6.

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The IIFE immediately calls itself with the current value of i, capturing it as j in a new scope.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: In the let solution, each iteration's callback forms a closure over its own block-scoped i. In the IIFE solution, the inner callback forms a closure over j (the IIFE's parameter). Closures are what allow each callback to remember its own value even though they all run after the loop completes.

g.text: A: It prints 6 6 6 6 6. All callbacks close over the same var i. By the time any callback executes, the loop is done and i is 6.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: How do you fix the above code?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Use let instead of var. let creates a new block-scoped binding for each iteration, so each callback closes over its own i. Alternatively, use an IIFE to create a new scope per iteration.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Why does let fix the problem?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: let is block-scoped. In a for loop, each iteration gets its own new binding of i. The setTimeout callback forms a closure over that unique binding.

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: No. Even with a 0ms delay, setTimeout defers execution to after the current call stack is empty (via the event loop). Synchronous code always runs before any timer callbacks.

g.text: This episode is a comprehensive closure interview drill. Each question builds on the previous, probing edge cases and practical applications. Mastering these questions covers the full spectrum of what interviewers ask about closures.

g.text: Q1: What is a Closure in JavaScript?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Answer: A closure is a function along with a reference to its outer (lexical) environment — i.e., the scope in which it was defined. A closure gives the function access to variables from its enclosing scope even after that scope has returned.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q2: Will the following code still form a closure?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Answer: Yes. The closure is formed at the moment inner is defined inside outer. It doesn't matter whether inner is returned or called internally — it still has access to x through its lexical environment. Sequence and call location don't affect closure formation.

g.text: Why this matters: The count variable cannot be directly modified from outside createCounter. External code must use the exposed methods. This is the module pattern — closure-based encapsulation.

g.text: Q9: What are the disadvantages of closures?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Over-consumption of memory: Closed-over variables are kept in memory as long as the closure exists. If many closures are created over large objects, memory usage grows.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Memory leaks: If closures are attached to event listeners or stored in long-lived collections without ever being removed, the referenced variables can never be garbage collected.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Browser freezing: In extreme cases, accumulated memory from many closures can degrade or freeze the browser.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Best practice: Remove event listeners when no longer needed. Set large closed-over variables to null when the closure is done using them to help garbage collection.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Episode 13: First Class Functions & Anonymous Functions

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Functions are first-class citizens in JavaScript — they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions. This flexibility is the foundation of functional programming.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript treats functions as first-class values. This means functions behave like any other value in the language — they can be stored, passed around, and returned. This episode covers all the ways to create and name functions, the distinctions that matter for hoisting and debugging, and what "first-class function" really means.

g.text: Q: What is the difference between a function statement and a function expression?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The major difference is hoisting. A function statement is fully hoisted — callable anywhere in its scope. A function expression assigns a function to a variable — only the variable is hoisted (as undefined), not the function. Calling it before the assignment throws a TypeError.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is an anonymous function?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: A function without a name. It must be used as a value — assigned to a variable, passed as an argument, or returned from another function. A standalone anonymous function is a SyntaxError.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is a named function expression?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: A function expression where the function also has a name. The name is only accessible inside the function (for recursion). It does not create an outer-scope binding. Named expressions are useful for debugging as the name appears in stack traces.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Functions are first-class when they can be used as values — assigned to variables, passed as arguments to other functions, and returned from functions. JavaScript functions are first-class citizens.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Named function expression = has a name visible only inside itself (not in outer scope)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Parameters = placeholders in definition; Arguments = actual values at call time

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: First-class functions = functions as values: assignable, passable, returnable

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Callbacks are the gateway to asynchronous JavaScript — they allow synchronous JS to hook into async operations. But they carry responsibilities: unused event listeners hold memory and can slow your page.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript is synchronous and single-threaded, yet it can handle timers, fetch API calls, and user interactions seemingly "at the same time." The mechanism that makes this possible is callbacks. A callback is simply a function passed to another function to be called later — often when an async operation completes.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Event listeners extend this pattern to DOM events and are a foundational browser API — but they come with a critical memory management concern.

g.text: Memory: Why You Must Remove Event Listeners

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Event listeners form closures — which means they keep referenced variables alive in memory. When an event listener is attached:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The callback function is stored in the Web API environment

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: If the callback closes over variables, those variables cannot be garbage collected

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Even if the Call Stack is idle, the listener persists

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This is especially problematic for scroll, click, mousemove listeners on pages with many elements — each active listener holds memory.

g.text: Q: What is a callback function?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: A callback is a function passed as an argument to another function, to be invoked at a later time — either immediately (synchronous callback) or after an async operation completes (async callback).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: How do callbacks enable asynchronous behavior in JavaScript?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: When an async operation (timer, network request, event) completes, the browser places the registered callback into the Callback Queue. The event loop moves it to the Call Stack when the stack is empty. This allows the main thread to remain free while waiting.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Why should you remove event listeners when they are no longer needed?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Event listeners form closures — they keep referenced variables in memory. Even when the Call Stack is idle, active event listeners persist in the Web API environment. Removing them with removeEventListener allows the garbage collector to free the associated memory.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Why are anonymous functions a problem for removeEventListener?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: removeEventListener requires the same function reference used in addEventListener. An anonymous function defined inline cannot be referenced again, so it cannot be removed — the listener is permanently stuck.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A callback is a function passed as an argument — to be called later

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Callbacks give JS access to the async world (timers, events, fetch)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Event listeners use callbacks and often form closures to maintain state

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Closures in event listeners keep variables alive — cannot be garbage collected while the listener is active

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Always removeEventListener when a listener is no longer needed (use named function references)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Heavy use of unremoved listeners (scroll, click, mousemove) on many elements can significantly slow a page

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The event loop is JavaScript's secret weapon — it coordinates the Call Stack, Web APIs, Callback Queue, and Microtask Queue to enable non-blocking async behavior in a single-threaded language.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript has a single Call Stack — it can only do one thing at a time. Yet browsers handle timers, network requests, and user events seemingly simultaneously. This is possible because JavaScript doesn't work alone: the browser runtime provides Web APIs, and the event loop continuously coordinates between the Call Stack and the various queues to process async work.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This is one of the most important and most-tested topics in JavaScript. Understanding it deeply will help you predict async behavior, debug race conditions, and write performant code.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Call Stack — executes code, one frame at a time

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Web APIs — setTimeout, fetch, DOM APIs, localStorage, console, Geolocation, Bluetooth, etc.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Callback Queue (Task Queue) — holds callbacks from Web APIs ready to run

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Microtask Queue — holds Promise callbacks and MutationObserver callbacks (higher priority)

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The event loop starts running immediately when the JS engine starts — it runs "forever" (or until the tab is closed).

g.text: If microtasks keep creating more microtasks (e.g., a .then() that schedules another .then() infinitely), the Callback Queue never gets a turn. This is called starvation — the callbacks in the Task Queue starve because microtasks never stop.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: When does the event loop actually start? The event loop runs continuously from the moment the JS engine starts. It is always running and always checking — it's an infinite loop that never stops.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Are synchronous callbacks (map, filter, reduce) registered in the Web API? No. Only asynchronous callbacks are registered with Web APIs. Synchronous callbacks like those passed to map, filter, and forEach execute immediately in the current Call Stack frame.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Do event listener callbacks get removed from Web API memory after one call? No. Event listener callbacks (click, scroll, etc.) stay in the Web API environment indefinitely. This is why it's important to explicitly removeEventListener when you're done. Timer callbacks (setTimeout) are one-shot — they're removed after firing.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What if setTimeout delay is 0ms? The callback still goes to the Callback Queue and must wait for the Call Stack to be empty. Even if the delay is 0ms, synchronous code runs first.

g.text: Q: What is the event loop?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The event loop is a continuously running mechanism that checks whether the Call Stack is empty and whether there is work in the Callback Queue or Microtask Queue. If the stack is empty, it moves the next item from a queue to the stack.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is the difference between the Callback Queue and the Microtask Queue?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The Microtask Queue has higher priority and holds Promise callbacks and MutationObserver callbacks. The Callback Queue (Task Queue) holds setTimeout/setInterval callbacks and event handler callbacks. The event loop always fully drains the Microtask Queue before processing the Callback Queue.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is starvation in the context of the event loop?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Starvation occurs when the Microtask Queue continuously generates new microtasks, preventing the Callback Queue from ever being processed. Callbacks in the Task Queue are "starved" of execution time.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: Can setTimeout(fn, 0) guarantee immediate execution after the current code?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: No. The callback goes to the Callback Queue. It will run only after: (a) the current synchronous code finishes, (b) the Call Stack is empty, and (c) the Microtask Queue is drained. Any pending microtasks (Promise callbacks) run first.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JS is single-threaded but the browser runtime provides Web APIs for async operations

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Callback Queue: setTimeout/event callbacks — lower priority

g.text: Episode 16: JS Engine Exposed — Google's V8 Architecture

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript runs everywhere — from smartwatches to servers — because of the JavaScript Runtime Environment. The V8 engine, written in C++, translates your high-level JS into machine code through parsing, compilation, and execution.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript can run on any device that has a JavaScript Runtime Environment (JRE). The heart of the JRE is the JS Engine — a piece of software (not hardware) that interprets and executes JavaScript. Understanding how the engine works — parsing to AST, JIT compilation, garbage collection — explains why JS is both flexible and fast.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Google's V8 is the most widely used JS engine, powering Chrome and Node.js. This episode exposes V8's internal architecture.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The JRE is a container that can run JavaScript code. It consists of:

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JS Engine — the core that executes JS (the heart of the JRE)

g.text: Set of APIs — to connect with the outside environment (browser, Node.js runtime)

g.text: ECMAScript is the governing body/specification that defines how JavaScript should behave. All JS engines must follow ECMAScript rules. The current version is ES2024 (ES15). This is why the same JS code runs consistently across all compliant engines.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The JS Engine Is Software, Not Hardware

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The JS engine is software written in a lower-level language (V8 is written in C++). It takes high-level JavaScript code and produces machine code that the computer's processor can execute.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The engine reads your JavaScript source code and breaks it down:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Tokenization (Lexical Analysis): Code is split into tokens — the smallest meaningful units.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Syntax Parsing: Tokens are analyzed for correct syntax and converted into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The AST is a tree data structure representing the program's structure

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Each node represents a construct (declaration, expression, statement)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Tools like astexplorer.net let you visualize the AST for any JS code

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript used to be purely interpreted (line by line, slow). Modern engines use JIT compilation — a hybrid approach:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Interpreter (Ignition in V8): Takes the AST and converts it to bytecode — an intermediate representation that starts executing immediately

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Compiler (TurboFan in V8): While the interpreter runs, the compiler monitors execution. Frequently executed code ("hot" code) is optimized — compiled to highly efficient machine code

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Deoptimization: If the compiler's assumptions turn out to be wrong (e.g., a variable type changes), V8 deoptimizes back to the interpreted version

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This combination delivers both fast startup (interpreter) and high peak performance (compiler).

g.text: V8 uses the Orinoco garbage collector, which employs the Mark and Sweep algorithm:

g.text: Mark: Starting from root references, traverse all reachable objects and mark them as "alive"

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Sweep: Any unmarked object (unreachable from roots) is considered garbage and its memory is freed

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This is why objects that are no longer referenced (and not closed over by active closures) are automatically cleaned up.

g.text: Q: What is a JavaScript Runtime Environment?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The JRE is a container that enables JavaScript to run. It includes the JS engine, Web/Node APIs, event loop, and queues. Different environments (browser, Node.js) have different JREs but all execute the same ECMAScript-compliant JS.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: ECMAScript is the specification (standard) that governs how JavaScript should behave. All JS engines must conform to ECMAScript. It defines the language's syntax, types, object model, and standard library.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Just-In-Time compilation is a hybrid approach combining interpretation and compilation. The interpreter starts executing immediately; the compiler monitors execution and optimizes frequently-run ("hot") code paths into efficient machine code at runtime.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: An AST is a tree-structured representation of the source code's syntactic structure. The parser generates it by analyzing tokens. The AST is then handed to the interpreter/compiler for code generation and optimization.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What are Ignition and TurboFan?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Ignition is V8's interpreter — it converts the AST to bytecode and begins execution. TurboFan is V8's optimizing compiler — it watches for "hot" code paths and compiles them to optimized machine code for speed.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What is the Mark and Sweep algorithm?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Mark and Sweep is V8's garbage collection algorithm. It marks all objects reachable from roots (Call Stack, globals), then sweeps away all unreachable (unmarked) objects — freeing their memory.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JRE = JS engine + APIs + event loop + queues; different per environment (browser, Node.js)

g.text: setTimeout guarantees a minimum delay — not an exact one. The callback cannot run until the Call Stack is empty, so a busy main thread makes timers lie.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Developers often assume that setTimeout(fn, 1000) will call fn in exactly 1000 milliseconds. This is not true. The delay is a minimum — the actual execution time depends on when the Call Stack becomes free. If the main thread is blocked with heavy synchronous work, the timer fires late — sometimes very late.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This episode demonstrates the problem concretely and reinforces JavaScript's most important rule: do not block the main thread.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Do not block the main thread.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: JavaScript is single-threaded — there is only one Call Stack. If it is busy running synchronous code, nothing else can happen: no timer callbacks, no event handlers, no rendering updates. The page appears frozen.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: setTimeout(fn, delay) guarantees that fn will not be called before delay milliseconds. It does not guarantee that fn will be called at delay milliseconds.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The actual execution time = delay + time spent waiting for Call Stack to empty.

g.text: The timer completed after 2 seconds (the Web API counted down correctly), but the callback was placed in the Callback Queue. The event loop couldn't move it to the Call Stack because the busy-wait loop was occupying it. By the time the loop finished and "End" printed, the callback finally got to run — ~10 seconds after being registered.

g.text: Q: Does setTimeout(fn, 1000) guarantee execution after exactly 1000ms?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: No. It guarantees the callback will not fire before 1000ms. The actual execution time is delay + time waiting for Call Stack to clear. If the main thread is busy, the callback fires late.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: What happens to a setTimeout callback when the main thread is blocked?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: The timer counts down correctly in the Web API environment. When the delay expires, the callback moves to the Callback Queue. But it can only run after the Call Stack becomes empty. If the main thread is blocked, the callback waits in the queue.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: It defers fn to the Callback Queue with a minimum delay of 0ms. It will execute only after all current synchronous code and all microtasks (Promises) have finished.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Q: How can you handle CPU-intensive work in the browser without blocking the main thread?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A: Use Web Workers — they run on a separate thread and can perform heavy computation without freezing the UI. Results are communicated back to the main thread via message passing.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: setTimeout provides a minimum delay guarantee — not a precise one

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The callback waits in the Callback Queue until the Call Stack is empty

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Blocking the main thread (long synchronous loops) delays all pending timers and event callbacks

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: setTimeout(fn, 0) still defers execution — synchronous code and microtasks run first

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The golden rule: never block the main thread — keep synchronous operations fast

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: For heavy computation: use Web Workers; for batching DOM updates: use requestAnimationFrame
